entries.title: The Mercy Step by Marcia Hutchinson audiobook review – a Caribbean child’s-eye view of 60s Bradford
entries.summary: The author captures the comedy and cruelty in this tenderly written coming-of-age taleThis Women’s prize-nominated novel from Marcia Hutchinson is told from the perspective of Mercy Hanson, a girl born in Bradford in 1962 to a mother she adores and a father she fears. We follow Mercy, their spirited fifth child, from birth through her toddler years to primary education. There she discovers books f
entries.content:
This Women’s prize-nominated novel from Marcia Hutchinson is told from the perspective of Mercy Hanson, a girl born in Bradford in 1962 to a mother she adores and a father she fears. We follow Mercy, their spirited fifth child, from birth through her toddler years to primary education. There she discovers books for the first time, in which she finds delicious escape.

In her first week at school, she flees the classroom and runs all the way home after a teacher inadvertently kicks her in the forehead and then denies it. This prompts her God-fearing mother to march to school and into the classroom where she threatens the teacher with hellfire if she touches her daughter again. But Mercy’s mother is unable to protect herself or her children from her short-tempered husband who is “very tall, a proper giant” and smokes Capstan Full Strength cigarettes. Mercy’s father slaps her in her crib when she cries, and viciously beats her mother.

The narrator is Hutchinson, whose reading draws out the comic and the unhappy elements of Mercy’s story and who moves seamlessly between her young protagonist’s Yorkshire tones and her mother’s Jamaican Patois. Tenderly written, with moments of sweetness and levity, the novel is named after the stair on which Mercy sits at home, clutching her beloved toy Dolly and surveying the goings on in the household. Her child’s-eye view of the world is effective here not only in showing us the preoccupations that shape childhood but in revealing the cost of the cruelty inflicted by adults.

Available via Recorded Books, 9hr 3min

Further listening

Famesick

Lena Dunham, 4th Estate, 11hr 46min

The creator of the hit millennial TV series Girls narrates her memoir in which she reflects on her career, controversies, relationships and addictions along with multiple health challenges which include OCD, early menopause and endometriosis.

Son of Nobody

Yann Martel, Canongate, 7hr 32min

Aaron Willis and Robin Wilcock are the narrators of this novel by the Life of Pi author. It tells of a Canadian classicist who stumbles across a lost epic poem about the Trojan war which is told from the perspective of a common soldier.

entries.title: What we’re reading: China Miéville, Sebastian Barry, Derek Owusu and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in September
entries.summary: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsI was sideswiped by Giada Scodellaro’s Ruins, Child. Echoes of a less elliptical b
entries.content:
China Miéville, author

I was sideswiped by Giada Scodellaro’s Ruins, Child. A brilliant, strange book that challenged me in the most exhilarating way, with its fractured language and dream-cinema visions, the sense it bestowed of walking through a corridor full of echoes. Echoes of a less elliptical but no-less political kind haunt Jordy Rosenberg’s astounding Night Night Fawn. I guess you could call it a family novel? But it’s at least as much about fascism as it is about the family – as well as about unsettling linkages between the two. And for horrors and rage in a nonfiction register, Jonas Marvin’s The Breaking of the English Working Class is an indispensable – and beautifully written – essay on decades of structural, economic and psychic violence. The feeling it provoked in me brought to mind John Berger’s phrase “undefeated despair”.

The Rouse by China Miéville is published by Picador (£35). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Linda, Guardian reader

I was totally immersed in Whale Fall by Elizabeth O’Connor, a beautifully written story describing a short time in the life of a young woman and her fishing community on an island off the coast of Wales in the 1930s. The simplicity of this tale is underpinned with intriguing moral issues when two anthropologists visit the island to study the lives and history of the islanders. The book is the most poetic I’ve read in a while.

Derek Owusu, author

I’ve enjoyed so many books recently. Two I now claim as favourites of all time. The first is Beloved by Toni Morrison. Incredibly late to the party because I was resistant to reading her again having had such a hard time with Sula. But Beloved, in my opinion, is the perfect novel. The second is Pedro Páramo by Juan Rulfo, one of the founding texts of the Latin American tradition of magical realism. It was hard work but so enjoyable, a reminder that challenging can be fun and that it’s possible to tell a story in a variety of ways. Last, I want to mention The Bridge of San Luis Rey by Thornton Wilder. I’ve only just finished it, so coherent feelings are still working themselves out, but in the mix I know there is admiration, pleasure, something life affirming and something ineffable sparked by the religious elements of the novel. I’m almost certain it’s going to join the others as one of my favourites. I’m having a great run.

The Recovery House by Derek Owusu is published by Merky Books (£16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Fiona, Guardian reader

In the day, Mario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin, a giant ship of a book which, at nearly a thousand pages, will probably steer me through the remains of 2026. In the night, when I cannot sleep, I do as I always do around the date of my birthday: a re-read of all of Jean Rhys. With her, I am on the moonlit deck of the ship and we watch the darkness of a deep sea rush by. For sanity, The Practice of Not Thinking by Ryunosuke Koike: the antidote to botched CBT therapy. For inspiration, For Now by Eileen Myles, concerning the loss of part of their archive and the struggle to hold on to a rent controlled apartment of 40 years. And My Life on the Road by Gloria Steinem. Of course.

Sebastian Barry, author

If anyone is in a mood to have their psyches calmed and their reading synapses restored, then The Last Chronicle of Barset by Anthony Trollope is the cat’s pyjamas. I was nodding my head recently when Marlon James was saying somewhere that he rated Trollope above Dickens. Not that D is any slouch. I am rereading a book I read for work, and now again just because it’s so excellently done, Army Life in a Black Regiment, by Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Emerson said it was a masterpiece by a writer not known for writing masterpieces(!) The Penguin Classics reissue in the late 1990s also has his correspondence with Emily Dickinson and an account of his one meeting with her, revelatory on many levels. She spoke as she wrote. I was also very admiring of a little book of poems by Kayleigh Jayshree called Mango and Starblush, which Miss Dickinson might have called true poems.

The Newer World by Sebastian Barry is published by Faber (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Dodge City by Patrick deWitt review – a wild draft-dodging road trip
entries.summary: This tale of a 60s college dropout driving across the US to avoid being sent to Vietnam is committed to both readerly pleasure and literary artificeCanadian author Patrick deWitt broke through with a western, 2011’s Booker-shortlisted The Sisters Brothers. Now, he has taken on another hallowed American genre: the road novel. Recent works by Miranda July and Ben Markovits have, in very different wa
entries.content:
Canadian author Patrick deWitt broke through with a western, 2011’s Booker-shortlisted The Sisters Brothers. Now, he has taken on another hallowed American genre: the road novel. Recent works by Miranda July and Ben Markovits have, in very different ways, used the idea of the road trip as a way to dramatise midlife crisis. As befits a writer who is, in so many ways, a throwback, Dodge City returns the genre to its roots: the 1960s, and youth as opposed to middle age. A short précis – a cross-country journey undertaken by a UCLA drop-out armed only with a bag of amphetamines – makes the book sound like an Easy Rider tribute. It is typical for deWitt novels to be compared to films rather than other books. But in this case, something very different transpires.

The novel opens with our protagonist, Leland “Lee” Clarke, receiving his draft notice – he is to be sent to Vietnam. He has just been expelled from UCLA for assaulting a fellow student, a rich hippy who condescends to him. This “event of violence” (a “one-punch wonder”, as Lee’s father calls it) costs him his draft deferment. Lee doesn’t consider himself a conscientious objector – that is only another form of heroism, and “the myth of the hero is at the heart of my critique of the entire exercise”. But nor does he want to go to Vietnam. He decides, instead, to dodge – to head to Canada. Younger readers may note with envy that being kicked out of college mattered a lot less when you weren’t tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt.

He has, in any case, been thinking of ending things with Cal, short for Calliope, the beautiful blond daughter of east coast intellectuals. Lee is the unglamorous product of a broken home in Concrete, Washington. Cal finds him exotic: “a patrician redneck”, meaning someone who irons his T-shirts. Over time, their class differences have begun to grate. The hippy he punches is a friend of Cal’s.

To raise money for the journey, he sells his own car and signs up to a “drive-away” service, delivering a brand-new Jaguar E-Type to its owner. Since he may be saying goodbye to his country for good, he plots an L-shaped route from Los Angeles to New Jersey that will allow him to say individual farewells to his father in Concrete, his mother in Montana, and his sister, a trainee nurse, in Manhattan. His brother Harry, in Minnesota, he plans to avoid. There is ancient history there.

DeWitt is a throwback because he has never been near a master of fine arts programme (he dropped out of high school) and because he writes what is unquestionably “literary fiction” for a large audience, and makes a living from doing so. To Chad Harbach’s dilemma for the young North American writer, “MFA v NYC”, deWitt’s triumphant answer is “neither”. You see this in his simultaneous commitment to readerly pleasure and literary artifice; and above all in his prose.

With his puns, archaisms, tics (“certain of the” for “some”), fondness for the passive voice and tendency to use two or three words more than strictly needed, deWitt violates almost every current MFA norm. Like one of his favourite writers, Ivy Compton-Burnett, he is a master of arch dialogue: more eloquent, and usually more enjoyable, than the naturalistic kind. DeWitt’s idiosyncrasies are not always euphonious – he can take his preference for Latin over Anglo-Saxon verbs to irritating lengths – but they remind us of the difference between having style and having a style.

Where deWitt is most contemporary is in his preoccupation with the past. Almost all his novels have historical settings, and his protagonists are stalked by old traumas. This is why Dodge City is no Easy Rider. If the essence of hippiedom is living in the present, and the special privilege of youth is ownership of the future, Lee Clarke’s business is with his past. The visits to his parents and siblings – in the end, he finds that he can’t avoid Harry – are not token goodbyes, but attempts to settle emotional accounts.

The journey itself is less one of self-discovery than of the reader discovering Lee, who is from the Hans Castorp school of hero. “Perfectly ordinary, if engaging” is how Thomas Mann described Hans. The reader sees Lee’s ordinariness right away, and over the course of the book grows more and more engaged. This is a deWitt novel, of course, and so the reader can expect – and is supplied with – vivid minor characters, hijinks, and a tone that lives confidently on the margin between silliness and misery.

Over the course of his career, however, deWitt has changed. His books have become more contemplative, less rambunctious; if he has always trafficked in real feelings in slightly unreal settings, the settings are growing realer, and the feelings softer. Dodge City is not exactly optimistic, but its emotional tendency is towards something few would have expected of the author of The Sisters Brothers: tenderness.

Dodge City by Patrick deWitt is published by HarperCollins (£18.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller London Falling shortlisted for Baillie Gifford prize
entries.summary: The acclaimed American journalist, who won the nonfiction prize in 2021, is shortlisted alongside Andrea Wulf and Matthew SweetFormer Baillie Gifford winner Patrick Radden Keefe is among the authors shortlisted for the 2026 prize, this time with his book on London’s criminal underbelly.The six-strong shortlist spans literary biography, ancient history, true crime and international reportage, with
entries.content:
Former Baillie Gifford winner Patrick Radden Keefe is among the authors shortlisted for the 2026 prize, this time with his book on London’s criminal underbelly.

The six-strong shortlist spans literary biography, ancient history, true crime and international reportage, with James Baldwin, Barbara Cartland and Alexander the Great among its subjects.

Keefe, who won the prize in 2021 for his book Empire of Pain, is this time selected for London Falling. This book tells the story of the death of Zac Brettler, a British teenager who fell from a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, described as “a scrupulously researched work of narrative nonfiction” and “grimly absorbing from start to finish” in Ian Thomson’s Guardian review.

Keefe is joined by Andrea Wulf – who was previously longlisted in 2008 – along with Nicholas Boggs, Matthew Sweet, Edmund Richardson and Anand Gopal. The winner, announced on 4 November, will receive £50,000.

Wulf has been recognised for a second time with The Traveller, which traces the life of George Forster, an 18th-century naturalist and explorer who joined Captain Cook’s second voyage around the world as a teenager.

Matthew Sweet’s The Great Dictator explores the life of the prolific romance novelist Barbara Cartland, who famously dictated the 723 novels she authored, against the backdrop of the changing sexual and social politics of her era. In a Guardian review, Kathryn Hughes wrote: “Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study.”

Edmund Richardson made the shortlist for his book Alexander, which charts the life of Alexander the Great. Meanwhile, Nicholas Boggs’ biography, Baldwin, reflects on the friendships, romances and creative relationships that influenced the writer’s work. Ralf Webb praised Boggs’s “exhaustive” research in his Guardian review, enabling the author to “meticulously re-stage Baldwin’s life in something like biographic ultra-high-definition”.

The final book on the shortlist, Anand Gopal’s Days of Love and Rage, examines the Syrian civil war through the experiences of residents of Manbij, a city in the country’s north.

Chair of judges Kirsty Lang said the books offer “something for everyone”. “It is an eclectic list united by stories of people navigating a world full of conflict as well as hope,” she said. “At a time when many of us are trying to make sense of a complex and frightening world, nonfiction can help us find our way through.”

The shortlist was drawn from a longlist of 13 books, including Murder in Paris ’68 by Edward Chisholm, The Nord Stream Conspiracy by Bojan Pancevski, Ukrainian Lessons by Charlotte Higgins, Redwood by Ben Macintyre, Hotel Exile by Jane Rogoyska, Never Say War by Åsne Seierstad and Stay Alive by Ian Buruma. The books were selected from more than 350 eligible titles published between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026.

Alongside Lang, the judges include novelist Elif Shafak, Waterstones head of books Bea Carvalho, writer and cultural historian Tiffany Jenkins, Spectator literary editor Sam Leith, and editor and reporter Ravi Mattu.

The prize was founded in 1999 as the Samuel Johnson prize, and has been sponsored by investment management firm Baillie Gifford since 2016. The firm has faced criticism over its investments in fossil fuels and companies with links to Israel. In 2024, campaign group Fossil Free Books organised boycotts of literary festivals sponsored by Baillie Gifford.

Last year’s prize was won by Australian writer Helen Garner for her collected diaries, How to End a Story.

  • To explore the shortlisted titles for the Baillie Gifford prize 2026, visit

    guardianbookshop.com.

entries.title: Missouri Williams and China Miéville among writers on ‘adventurous’ Goldsmiths shortlist
entries.summary: Six writers are in contention for the £10,000 books prize, which celebrates fiction that ‘breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form’Missouri Williams, China Miéville and Polly Barton are among the writers shortlisted for this year’s Goldsmiths prize.The £10,000 award recognises fiction that “breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form”.Explore the shortlis
entries.content:
Missouri Williams, China Miéville and Polly Barton are among the writers shortlisted for this year’s Goldsmiths prize.

The £10,000 award recognises fiction that “breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form”.

Judging chair Francis Spufford, novelist and professor of creative writing at Goldsmiths, University of London, said the judges had found “newness of many different kinds” in this year’s submissions, adding: “We enjoyed ourselves, and we enjoyed being challenged.”

Williams was shortlisted for her Booker-longlisted novel The Vivisectors, set in an unnamed university town where academics and a group of gardeners are locked in a power struggle. In a Guardian review, Ian Maleney wrote: “Williams writes with a singular brand of Ballardian ferocity – she revels in the wretched and the craven.”

Miéville’s The Rouse, an epic 1,200-page paranormal novel 20 years in the making, was described in Stuart Kelly’s Guardian review as “affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frightening”.

The shortlist features two debuts, including the first novel from translator and nonfiction author Barton. What Am I, a Deer? follows a young woman who moves to Frankfurt to work for a video game company and becomes fixated on a man she encounters on her commute. It was described in a Guardian review as “a piercing study of yearning, and of the modern condition of feeling perpetually on the verge of one’s own life”.

Also on the shortlist is Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa, one of two Irish authors on the shortlist and the author of A Ghost in the Throat. The book explores the history of women incarcerated in a Cork asylum, and was described by Brian Dillon in his Guardian review as a work of “extraordinary formal and ethical force”.

Another Irish author, Keith Ridgway, is shortlisted for Dooneen, which paints a picture of social unrest in Dublin. It is an “appealingly labyrinthine novel” featuring “wonderfully absorbing and offbeat comedy”, according to Michael Donkor’s Guardian review.

Completing the shortlist is another debut, Aea Varfis-Van Warmelo’s Attention-Seeking Behaviour, which is narrated by a compulsive liar and combines fiction with memoir and essay. Judge David Sexton said the book brings “brio worthy of a Muriel Spark heroine to telling us what she thinks we should know about her promiscuous, deceitful life in London now”.

“The Goldsmiths prize exists to remind us that the novel, as the name suggests, is new,” Spufford said. “It may be 300 years old, but in adventurous hands, it still has limitless possibilities as a form.”

The judging panel also includes writer and translator Kate Briggs, novelist Hari Kunzru and journalist and former Evening Standard literary editor David Sexton.

Tanjil Rashid, culture editor at the New Statesman said: “A spirit of experimentation and freedom has been central to the novel and its enduring appeal; all of these books have that.”

The winner will be announced at a ceremony at Foyles on Charing Cross Road in London on 4 November.

Last year’s prize was won by CD Rose for We Live Here Now. Previous winners of the prize, which was launched in 2013 in association with the New Statesman and is now in its 14th year, include Rachel Cusk, Eimear McBride, Ali Smith, Isabel Waidner and Benjamin Myers.

entries.title: On the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli review – a physicist’s guide to life, the universe and everything
entries.summary: Near-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselvesUnder the letter “B” in the index at the back of Carlo Rovelli’s latest book you will find Francis Bacon, bats, behaviourism, Henri Bergson, and the big bang. This intriguing little miscellany reflects the sweeping ambition of what is perhaps Rovelli’s most overtly philosophical work t
entries.content:
Under the letter “B” in the index at the back of Carlo Rovelli’s latest book you will find Francis Bacon, bats, behaviourism, Henri Bergson, and the big bang. This intriguing little miscellany reflects the sweeping ambition of what is perhaps Rovelli’s most overtly philosophical work to date.

Rovelli, who directs a quantum gravity research group in Marseille, has written several books on physics for the general reader, including the global bestseller Seven Brief Lessons on Physics. His latest is an attempt to integrate principles and theories from the discipline into a broader Weltanschauung: one of the essential unity of all things, and the profoundly relational and perspectival nature of the universe. “Electrons and minds, stones and laws, judgments and galaxies do not essentially differ in nature from one another,” he writes. “They are notions that illuminate each other.”

If this sounds familiar, that’s because it is. Rovelli echoes concepts that have been around for millennia in ancient thought, including Hinduism and Buddhism, from whose sacred texts he quotes. But what sets him apart from the countless other modern writers, dreamers and thinkers who preach the oneness of it all is that he grounds his ideas in scientific theory rather than theology or new age conjecture.

On the Equality of All Things is a slender volume holding an extraordinary density of ideas. Translator Simon Carnell, himself a poet, maintains the clarity and concision we have come to expect from Rovelli’s writing. In six chapters, or “lessons”, Rovelli lays out the philosophical significance of what he believes is a major scientific revolution, happening right now. The first lesson refers to his theory of relational quantum mechanics to ask us to abandon the notion that the world is made up of things with fixed properties. Rather, physical systems have properties relative to other physical systems. Also, everything’s moving, all the time, and there’s no fixed point around which we are in motion.

The second lesson takes aim at the idea of linearity. Rovelli urges us to accept circularity and question the need to identify the ultimate foundation of things, when in fact, it’s turtles all the way down. The lessons continue. The world is not made up of things at all, but processes. “Even a stone is a process”, and so are we. Time itself is mutable and passes at different speeds in different places. Our knowledge of anything can only ever be partial.

It’s enough to give you vertigo, and Rovelli admits it. “The resulting image of reality is haunting. Every fact is only a fact relative to something else, and even the fact that a fact is relative to something else is itself relative. There is no ground floor.” Yet, in contrast to the bleakness that can shroud such unflinching scientific accounts of the universe, Rovelli’s telling validates our messy, subjective human experiences. “None of this prevents us from describing the world from one perspective. Ours.” But the physics tells us that our perspectives are just that, and that there may be others.

On the Equality of All Things takes its place as part of a blossoming movement that asks us to see the world as a set of interconnected relationships. As such, it sits alongside the work of mycologist Merlin Sheldrake, botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, physiologist Denis Noble and nature writer Robert Macfarlane. Rovelli’s emphasis on perspective and relationality in physics echoes similar intellectual turns in social anthropology, ecology and biology that invite us to stop thinking about the world as something we stand without, and instead take our rightful place within it. Distancing himself from the more hubristic elements of the Enlightenment – an emphasis on certainty, linearity, and overconfidence in the imperfect instrument that is Reason – Rovelli asks us to embrace “the nimble lightness of circularity, complexity, ambiguity, metaphors, emotions, the acceptance of uncertainty and change”.

His refusal to denigrate human culture as being inferior to or incompatible with hard science is refreshing. He observes wryly that the term “consciousness” has superseded the word “soul” because it is perceived to be more scientific, even though it is just as nebulous. Provided we understand that physical processes underlie everything, Rovelli sees no reason why we may not “calmly speak of the soul and emotions just as we speak of tables even if tables are collections of atoms”.

For all Rovelli is a gifted communicator, some of the science in this book required a level of intellectual scaffolding that, alas, my rusty physics A-level did not provide. At his explanation of loop quantum gravity, my brain started to creak and let off steam. Yet, even if you don’t have the foggiest idea what the granularity of spacetime means, engaging with this book as an internally coherent work of philosophy and literature is rewarding enough. And Rovelli’s conclusion is powerful: we are physical systems dancing among other physical systems, and the world “is our blood brother”. We’re at home, among family. Perhaps it’s time we honoured that kinship.

entries.title: Dèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in Miami
entries.summary: The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier worksDèy, Edwidge Danticat’s first novel in over a decade, begins with a bang. Magnolia, the daughter of Haitian parents now shopping for a birthday present for her own daughter, hears gunfire, maybe bombs, in a Miami mall. A killer is on the loose – a young man high on hate, the author of online
entries.content:
Dèy, Edwidge Danticat’s first novel in over a decade, begins with a bang. Magnolia, the daughter of Haitian parents now shopping for a birthday present for her own daughter, hears gunfire, maybe bombs, in a Miami mall. A killer is on the loose – a young man high on hate, the author of online screeds about how “our country is under attack”, obsessed by cane toads who’ve been coming in from the Amazon basin. As she scrambles to the floor of a restaurant called Oasis, surrounded by dozens of diners playing dead, a man asks, “Is this a mass grave?”

Things have always been tough for Magnolia. Her mother chases pigeons by day, sleepwalks at night, is on and off lithium. Her father worked for many years as a bus driver in Brooklyn, saving every cent so he could buy a nice retirement home back in Haiti. She was brought up by an “aunt” whose family had been killed by goons employed by Haiti’s dictator-in-chief Papa Doc Duvalier. Later she gets to college, where “school was my refuge”.

Magnolia makes it out of the mall alive but finds herself rattled. Why can’t she tell the father of her child about what she witnessed? She doesn’t confide in her work colleagues either. At a pool party she almost has a seizure when a friend playfully sprays her with a water gun. Is this trauma? She has often felt brittle – finding a photo of herself in her early 20s, when she was a new mother, she says her eyes “look like headlights in a staring contest with a deer” – but now the ground beneath her feet feels especially shaky.Her anxieties – about her daughter’s future, her parents’ health – keep mounting.

Violence in Dèy isn’t confined to the mall. It runs through the news stories about Ramallah and Yemen and Congo that Magnolia follows. The reports she hears of daily life in Haiti, where gangs abduct young girls, torch homes, storm schools and even churches, prompt fears for the home her father has worked so hard to build. Then, both in the background and in everyone’s face, there is the US president himself, with his poisonous thought-blurts about Haitians eating dogs and coming from a “shithole” country.

Danticat, a sometime travel writer, is at her most appealing in her commemorations of Miami’s Little Haiti, a weathered world full of bakeries and barbershops, churches and religious stores, beauticians whose clientele watch Nollywood movies and read old copies of Ebony. But these hubs are being priced out by fusion restaurants and pilates studios. Magnolia works in property and is an agent of the displacements she and her colleagues bemoan.

Magnolia’s job attunes her not just to the economics but to the poetics of place. Her ears prick up when someone describes Haiti as “down there” or, in the case of her boss, “‘over there’, as though she were looking at its distant shores from the upper deck of a cruise ship”. A short but powerful chapter is devoted to the backstory of a Haitian security guard who was killed at the mall: after the 2010 earthquake he moved to Brazil to build stadiums for the 2016 Olympics, then on to Chile and Colombia, before braving swamps and mountains to get to the US/ Mexico border and low-paid jobs loading trucks, allowing him to send money to his siblings back home.

These peripheral characters are more vivid than Magnolia herself, who remains a wan, disassociated narrator throughout. Her language is sometimes academic (she describes her own daughter as “a liminal creature”), sometimes straight from a lifestyle magazine (“flaxen-tressed Black woman”). Motifs are spelled out for hard-of-hearing readers (“houses have always fascinated me, not only as physical structures, but as ideas, stories”) or in the manner of reading-group prompts (“We don’t always choose where we call home. Sometimes it’s others who decide”). The churn in her head – the violence that terrifies her – emerges in the tamest, most gentrified prose imaginable.

In the end, Dèy, which is set in 2018, reads like a tribute to 1990s postcolonial fiction. There are nods to the spectral (“I was sure my mother was a ghost”), riffs on “sympathetic pain” and “somatic knowledge” (“My period came for the first time on another September 11”), too much dining-table diplomacy. “Visual clutter bothers me,” admits Magnolia at one point; this novel – so tasteful, so scented – could do with more noise, smears, life.

entries.title: The Fall of the West by Owen Jones review – a bracing history of the changing world order
entries.summary: A journalist charts a quarter century of geopolitical hubris and economic overreach Like many Britons born in the 1980s, the journalist and Guardian columnist Owen Jones came of age with Tony Blair’s platitudes ringing in his ears. Politics at the turn of the millennium was a story of temporary dispensations mistaken for eternal truths: the definitive triumph of free market ideology; US military s
entries.content:
Like many Britons born in the 1980s, the journalist and Guardian columnist Owen Jones came of age with Tony Blair’s platitudes ringing in his ears. Politics at the turn of the millennium was a story of temporary dispensations mistaken for eternal truths: the definitive triumph of free market ideology; US military supremacy; a rules-based global order. As Jones recounts in his new book, these certainties would come crashing down over the next quarter of a century amid a succession of economic failures, foreign policy disasters and political crises.

Indeed, “the west” itself – as a shorthand for the US plus the wealthier western European nations – feels almost quaint today, given the increasing unilateralism of the administration in Washington. But in the 2000s it was part of the lexicon, as if the hemisphere were a political actor in its own right. Revisiting the US-led wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, we are reminded not just of their horrific death tolls (totalling half a million, by conservative estimates) but also their total strategic failure; the 2021 evacuation of Kabul airport, Jones writes, was “among the starkest images of American decline yet broadcast to the world”.

In addition to destabilising the region, these interventions weakened the foundations of the international legal system. As Jones points out, a precedent was set when Nato bombed Yugoslavia without UN security council authorisation in 1999; the 2003 invasion of Iraq, also without authorisation, further undermined the UN. So when Vladimir Putin subsequently invaded Ukraine on his own dubious pretext, western objections could be dismissed as hypocrisy. Perhaps the most ignominious example of western indifference to the international rule of law was Keir Starmer’s limp assertion that Israel had the “right” to cut off water and electricity to 2 million civilians in Gaza – a war crime – in retaliation for Hamas’s attacks on 7 October 2023.

Alongside these geopolitical catastrophes, Jones tells a story of domestic decline, of western economies built on chronic insecurity and precarious employment. In the 2000s, Thatcherite policies pursued by New Labour fleeced the public: “Essential services [were] turned into assets designed to generate returns. Passengers paid more for overcrowded trains. Rivers and seas were fouled while water companies loaded themselves with debt and paid out dividends.” Then came the 2008 financial crisis and the bankers’ bailout, paid for by austerity. In Britain and elsewhere, Jones notes a “correlation between the inability of centrist governments to tackle economic decline in any meaningful way, and the rise of the far right”.

The book is interspersed with snippets of interviews with an assortment of eyewitnesses, journalists, scholars and activists. They include the director of Iraq national museum in Baghdad, a former Lehman Brothers employee, a former head of the Afghan Red Crescent, the Greek economist Yanis Varoufakis, and the conservative commentator Andrew Sullivan, a repentant cheerleader for the Iraq war, who admits: “I was wrong on the major issues, on the morality of it and the practicality of it and the reason for it.”

Much of this terrain – Bush and Blair’s wars, the financial crash, the populist surge – has been extensively covered. The average well-informed reader will learn nothing new, but it is bracing to see what was once the news cycle take its place in the sweep of history, and Jones’s focus on free-market fundamentalism provides a compelling through-line. He suggests the second Trump administration, in all its cynical venality, is “the logical endpoint” of that philosophy. And he reminds us that the aggressive privatisation of the Russian economy in the 1990s brought terrible economic hardship which ultimately fuelled Putin’s revanchist nationalism.

For decades, electorates have been mis-sold a fanatical ideology: the prerogatives of the private sector must override the collective interest, and anything less is tantamount to Stalinism. This remains orthodoxy, but the rise to prominence of Zohran Mamdani, the avowedly socialist mayor of New York, offers a glimmer of hope to those who, like Jones, would prefer a society built on “common provision, democratic power, mutual obligation and the recognition that our fates are bound together”.
